turns.prompt_text: I have a lot of PLA for my 3D printer. I was wondering, could I just paint them a different color, say white? Would I need to use any special paint, or are there any good materials to use?
turns.response_html:
Painting PLA is a great way to customize your prints without constantly swapping filament rolls. Since PLA is a plastic with a relatively slick surface, the key to a professional finish is all in the surface preparation.

1. Preparation: The Most Important Step

Because of the "layer lines" inherent to 3D printing, paint tends to highlight imperfections rather than hide them.

  • Sanding: Start with a coarse grit (around 200) to knock down the ridges, then move to a finer grit (400 or 600) for a smooth finish.
  • Cleaning: After sanding, wash the part with dish soap and water to remove oils from your hands and plastic dust. Paint will not bond to a dusty surface.

2. Priming: Don't Skip It

You should almost always use a Primer before applying color.

  • Filler Primer: This is a "cheat code" for 3D printing. It is a thick spray primer (found at most hardware stores in the automotive section) that fills in the tiny gaps between layer lines.
  • Plastic-Specific Primer: Look for brands like Rust-Oleum or Krylon that explicitly state they "bond to plastic." This ensures the paint won't flake off later.

3. Recommended Paint Types

Once the piece is primed, you have a few excellent options for achieving a clean white finish:

  • Acrylic Spray Paints: These are the most common and easiest to use. Apply in multiple thin coats rather than one thick one to avoid drips.
  • Acrylic Hobby Paints: If you are painting fine details by hand (like for a model or a custom enclosure), brands like Vallejo or Citadel work beautifully on primed PLA.
  • Spray Enamels: These provide a very durable, hard shell, but they take much longer to dry and can sometimes react poorly if the primer isn't fully cured.

4. Finishing Touches

If the object will be handled frequently—like a tool handle or a mechanical part—apply a Clear Coat (Matte, Satin, or Gloss) once the white paint is dry. This protects the color from chipping and UV yellowing.

A quick tip for "Success with White": White is one of the hardest colors to get full coverage with. If you are painting over a very dark PLA (like black or navy), it is highly recommended to use a light gray primer first. It provides a neutral base that helps the white pigment pop without needing ten layers of paint.

Since you're working with a lot of material, are you planning on painting a single large assembly or a series of smaller, detailed components?
